lead: A buck converter steps a DC voltage down. A switch chops the input. An inductor and capacitor average the pulses, so the output is smooth and lower than the input. The diode gives inductor current a path when the switch opens. Gain comes from the duty ratio D, not a lossy resistor. Buck converters sit inside phone chargers, laptop adapters, LED drivers and processor regulators, turning 12 V or 24 V into 5 V, 3.3 V or 1.2 V efficiently.
prereq: You need Chapter 3.1 for duty ratio and continuous conduction, Chapter 3.2 for the filter in a switched-mode supply, and Unit 2 for capacitor filtering.

sections.h3: The circuit and the two states

blocks.text: The buck converter has source V<sub>s</sub>, switch S, freewheeling diode D<sub>f</sub>, inductor L, capacitor C and load resistor R. S and D<sub>f</sub> sit before the L-C filter. Output V<sub>o</sub> is across C and R.

When S is ON for T<sub>on</sub>, the input connects to L and the diode is reverse biased. Inductor voltage is v<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>s</sub> − V<sub>o</sub>. Inductor current i<sub>L</sub> rises. L stores energy and feeds C and R. When S is OFF for T<sub>off</sub>, i<sub>L</sub> cannot stop instantly. The diode turns on and gives i<sub>L</sub> a path. L is now between ground and the output, so v<sub>L</sub> = −V<sub>o</sub>. Current falls and L supplies the load.

blocks.where: v<sub>L</sub> is inductor voltage in volts; L is inductance in henries; i<sub>L</sub> is inductor current in amperes; t is time in seconds.

blocks.text: The inductor integrates this voltage. In steady state the average voltage across L over one period T is zero; otherwise current would drift each cycle. C holds V<sub>o</sub> nearly constant because C is large and f<sub>s</sub> is high. With V<sub>s</sub> = 50 V and V<sub>o</sub> = 20 V, current ramps up for 4 µs and down for 6 µs, as the figure shows.

Apply volt-second balance. During ON, volt-seconds are (V<sub>s</sub> − V<sub>o</sub>)T<sub>on</sub> = (V<sub>s</sub> − V<sub>o</sub>)DT. During OFF they are (−V<sub>o</sub>)(1−D)T. Their sum is zero.

blocks.where: V<sub>s</sub> is input voltage in volts; V<sub>o</sub> is average output voltage in volts; D = T<sub>on</sub>/T is duty ratio, unitless, 0 ≤ D ≤ 1; T is switching period in seconds; T<sub>on</sub> is on-time in seconds.
V<sub>o</sub> is average output voltage in volts; V<sub>s</sub> is input voltage in volts; D is duty ratio, unitless.

blocks.text: Divide by T: D(V<sub>s</sub> − V<sub>o</sub>) = (1−D)V<sub>o</sub>, so V<sub>o</sub> = D V<sub>s</sub>. Since D ≤ 1, V<sub>o</sub> ≤ V<sub>s</sub>. Buck only steps down. Duty ratio sets output; the switch does not burn excess as heat like a linear regulator.

A real diode has forward drop V<sub>D</sub>. During OFF, v<sub>L</sub> = −(V<sub>o</sub> + V<sub>D</sub>). Balance gives D(V<sub>s</sub> − V<sub>o</sub>) = (1−D)(V<sub>o</sub> + V<sub>D</sub>), so V<sub>o</sub> ≈ D V<sub>s</sub> − (1−D)V<sub>D</sub>. The drop lowers output, worst at low V<sub>o</sub>. A synchronous buck replaces the diode with a MOSFET. Its low on-resistance gives less drop, common for low-voltage high-current rails.

At light load the inductor current can reach zero before the period ends. This is discontinuous conduction mode (DCM). Then V<sub>o</sub> rises above D V<sub>s</sub> toward V<sub>s</sub>. The gain V<sub>o</sub> = D V<sub>s</sub> holds only in continuous conduction mode (CCM).

sections.h3: Ripple, peak current and design limits

blocks.text: During ON, di<sub>L</sub>/dt = (V<sub>s</sub> − V<sub>o</sub>)/L. Over T<sub>on</sub> = DT the current rises by ΔI<sub>L</sub> = (V<sub>s</sub> − V<sub>o</sub>)DT/L. Put V<sub>o</sub> = D V<sub>s</sub>: V<sub>s</sub> − V<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>(1−D), and V<sub>s</sub>(1−D)D = V<sub>o</sub>(1−D). So ΔI<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>o</sub>(1−D)/(f<sub>s</sub> L), with T = 1/f<sub>s</sub>.

blocks.where: ΔI<sub>L</sub> is peak-to-peak inductor current ripple in amperes; f<sub>s</sub> is switching frequency in hertz; L is inductance in henries; T is period in seconds.

blocks.text: Average inductor current equals load current I<sub>o</sub>. Peak and minimum are i<sub>max</sub> = I<sub>o</sub> + ΔI<sub>L</sub>/2 and i<sub>min</sub> = I<sub>o</sub> − ΔI<sub>L</sub>/2. For CCM, i<sub>min</sub> > 0. Set i<sub>min</sub> = 0 for the boundary: I<sub>o</sub> = ΔI<sub>L</sub>/2 = V<sub>o</sub>(1−D)/(2 f<sub>s</sub> L). Rearrange L<sub>min</sub> = (1−D)V<sub>o</sub>/(2 f<sub>s</sub> I<sub>o</sub>). If L is below L<sub>min</sub> at that load, the converter enters DCM.

C filters the triangular inductor current. Output ripple is ΔV<sub>o</sub> = ΔI<sub>L</sub>/(8 f<sub>s</sub> C). This assumes an ideal capacitor and CCM. Real electrolytic capacitors have ESR, adding a step ΔI<sub>L</sub> × ESR. Ceramic capacitors have low ESR for tight outputs.

Design steps: choose D = V<sub>o</sub>/V<sub>s</sub>; choose f<sub>s</sub> high enough to shrink L and C; choose L above L<sub>min</sub> for the lowest load that must stay in CCM; choose C for the allowed ΔV<sub>o</sub>; check capacitor ESR and diode or MOSFET drop. Larger L lowers ripple and peak current but slows transient response.

figure.caption: Inductor current for the worked example at D = 0.4: it ramps from 3.4 A to 4.6 A during the 4 µs on-time and falls back during the 6 µs off-time; the average is 4 A.

spec.aria: Inductor current ramps up during the on-time and down during the off-time, oscillating between 3.4 A and 4.6 A around a 4 A average.

examples.question: A buck converter has V<sub>s</sub> = 50 V, D = 0.4, f<sub>s</sub> = 100 kHz, L = 100 µH, C = 220 µF and a 5 Ω load. Find V<sub>o</sub>, the inductor ripple, the peak and minimum inductor current, the output ripple, and the inductance at the CCM boundary.
steps: Output voltage: V<sub>o</sub> = D·V<sub>s</sub> = 0.4 × 50 V = 20 V.
Load current: I<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>o</sub>/R = 20 V / 5 Ω = 4 A.
Period: T = 1/f<sub>s</sub> = 1/(100 kHz) = 10 µs. On-time: T<sub>on</sub> = D·T = 0.4 × 10 µs = 4 µs.
Inductor ripple: ΔI<sub>L</sub> = (V<sub>s</sub> − V<sub>o</sub>)·T<sub>on</sub>/L = (50 − 20) V × 4 µs / 100 µH = 1.2 A.
Peak current: i<sub>max</sub> = I<sub>o</sub> + ΔI<sub>L</sub>/2 = 4 A + 0.6 A = 4.6 A. Minimum: i<sub>min</sub> = 4 A − 0.6 A = 3.4 A. Since i<sub>min</sub> > 0, the converter is in CCM.
Output ripple: ΔV<sub>o</sub> = ΔI<sub>L</sub>/(8 f<sub>s</sub> C) = 1.2 A / (8 × 100 kHz × 220 µF) = 6.8 mV.
CCM boundary: L<sub>min</sub> = (1−D)V<sub>o</sub>/(2 f<sub>s</sub> I<sub>o</sub>) = (0.6 × 20 V)/(2 × 100 kHz × 4 A) = 15 µH. The 100 µH inductor is safely above this.
examples.answer: V<sub>o</sub> = 20 V, I<sub>o</sub> = 4 A, ΔI<sub>L</sub> = 1.2 A, i<sub>L</sub> swings between 3.4 A and 4.6 A, ΔV<sub>o</sub> = 6.8 mV, and L<sub>min</sub> = 15 µH, so the 100 µH inductor keeps the converter in CCM.
examples.check:
Vs = 50.0
D = 0.4
fs = 100e3
L = 100e-6
C = 220e-6
R = 5.0
Vo = D * Vs
Io = Vo / R
T = 1 / fs
Ton = D * T
dIL = (Vs - Vo) * Ton / L
imax = Io + dIL / 2
imin = Io - dIL / 2
dV = dIL / (8 * fs * C)
Lmin = (1 - D) * Vo / (2 * fs * Io)
print(Vo)
print(Io)
print(dIL)
print(imax)
print(imin)
print(round(dV * 1000, 1))
print(round(Lmin * 1e6, 1))

traps: V<sub>o</sub> = D·V<sub>s</sub> is a CCM result. In DCM the output floats upward toward V<sub>s</sub> as load lightens; do not use the gain formula at no load.
During on-time the inductor voltage is V<sub>s</sub> − V<sub>o</sub>, not V<sub>s</sub>. Forgetting the output term overestimates gain and ripple.
Duty ratio is unitless. T<sub>on</sub> and T must use the same unit: 4 µs / 10 µs, not 4 µs / 100 kHz.
Average inductor current is I<sub>o</sub>; peak is I<sub>o</sub> + ΔI<sub>L</sub>/2. Peak switch current equals peak inductor current.

quiz.q: Define the duty ratio D of a buck converter.
quiz.a: D = T<sub>on</sub>/T = T<sub>on</sub>·f<sub>s</sub>, the fraction of the switching period for which the switch is on. It is unitless and lies between 0 and 1.

quiz.q: Why must the freewheeling diode conduct when the switch opens?
quiz.a: Inductor current cannot change instantly. Without the diode path, inductor voltage would spike and damage the switch. The diode gives current a path, so v<sub>L</sub> becomes −V<sub>o</sub> and current falls smoothly.

quiz.q: A buck converter has V<sub>s</sub> = 24 V, D = 0.6, f<sub>s</sub> = 50 kHz, L = 200 µH and I<sub>o</sub> = 2 A. Find V<sub>o</sub> and ΔI<sub>L</sub>.
A buck converter designed for CCM at full load is run at 5 % load with the same duty ratio. What happens to V<sub>o</sub>?
quiz.a: Inductor current may reach zero before the period ends, so the converter enters DCM. In DCM output rises above D·V<sub>s</sub> toward V<sub>s</sub>. The controller must reduce D to hold V<sub>o</sub>.

quiz.q: What is the function of the capacitor C in a buck converter?
quiz.a: C holds output nearly constant, supplies the load during switching transitions and filters inductor ripple. Its ripple is ΔV<sub>o</sub> = ΔI<sub>L</sub>/(8 f<sub>s</sub> C) for an ideal capacitor.

quiz.q: Why does a synchronous buck replace the diode with a MOSFET, and where is it used?
quiz.a: A MOSFET has lower conduction drop than a diode at low output voltage and high current, so efficiency improves. It is used in processor and GPU regulators and battery-powered devices. Dead time is needed to avoid shoot-through.

quiz.q: Write the formula for the CCM boundary inductance L<sub>min</sub>.
quiz.a: L<sub>min</sub> = (1−D)V<sub>o</sub>/(2 f<sub>s</sub> I<sub>o</sub>). Below this value at the given load, the converter enters DCM.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production buck converters are often multiphase: interleaved stages cut ripple and share current in CPU regulators. Wide-bandgap GaN switches push f<sub>s</sub> into the MHz range, shrinking L and C. Digital controllers adapt D cycle by cycle. Search 'synchronous buck', 'multiphase VRM', 'GaN DC-DC' and 'peak current mode control'.
